eligibility_reason: The paper reports new-data (824 MTurk participants), preregistered close replications of Studies 1 and 2 of Hsee and Zhang (2004, JPSP) on distinction bias, with results reported per study and per hypothesis.

effects.original_title: Distinction bias: Misprediction and mischoice due to joint evaluation
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.outcome: Predicted happiness (1-9) for quantitatively different scenarios (80 vs 160 vs 240 buyers of one's poem book)
effects.contrast: Joint evaluation (within-subject differences between 80/160/240 buyers) vs separate evaluation (between-group differences between the same scenarios)
effects.description: Original Study 1: people in joint evaluation overpredict the difference in happiness between quantitatively different outcomes (80, 160, 240 buyers of their poem book) relative to people in separate evaluation, who rate these scenarios similarly.
effects.citation_sentence: In the present paper, we report replications and extensions of Studies 1 and 2 from Hsee and Zhang (2004).
effects.evidence: Study 1 Results: "Therefore, people in JE overpredicted the difference between the 80, 160, and 240 buyers scenarios."; "the results of Study 1 in the present paper support the theory of distinction bias and successfully replicate the results of Study 1 from Hsee and Zhang (2004)."; General Discussion: "Taken together, the results of Study 1 fully replicated the original findings."
effects.notes: Original DOI not given in full: references.json lists only the shortDOI 10/dhnrdb, so original_url left blank. Unit of coding: the original Study 1 reported two hypotheses as separate findings (H1 overprediction for quantitative differences; H2 no overprediction for qualitative differences; Table S3), so coded as two rows; a coder treating 'distinction bias in Study 1' as one claim would merge s1 rows (both success). Replication type: authors call these 'close'/'very close replications' (LeBel taxonomy) with 'incidental' differences: MTurk adults instead of US students, online Qualtrics instead of lab -> population and setting change -> close extension per codebook; 'direct' is a plausible alternative given the authors' framing. The 160-buyer reference-point extension conditions are a new test (not an original finding) and get no row.

effects.original_title: Distinction bias: Misprediction and mischoice due to joint evaluation
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.outcome: Predicted happiness (1-9) for qualitatively different scenarios (0 vs 80 buyers)
effects.contrast: Joint evaluation (within-subject 0 vs 80 buyers) vs separate evaluation (between-group 0 vs 80 buyers)
effects.description: Original Study 1: people in joint evaluation do not overpredict the happiness difference between qualitatively different outcomes (no buyers vs 80 buyers), since separate evaluators also rate 80 buyers significantly happier than none.
effects.citation_sentence: In the present paper, we report replications and extensions of Studies 1 and 2 from Hsee and Zhang (2004).
effects.evidence: Study 1 Results: "Thus, people in JE did not overpredict the difference in happiness between the 0 and 80 buyers scenarios."; Supplement: "We can conclude that the replication results aligned with the original also for the qualitatively different scenarios."
effects.notes: The claim is an absence-of-overprediction claim (original H2); both JE and SE differences were significant in the same direction in the replication, and JE actually underpredicted relative to SE, which the authors call consistent with the original. Replication effect sizes larger than original (d 2.60 vs 1.17 JE; 4.13 vs 3.26 SE) but authors still frame as aligned. See s1:quantitative row for DOI and replication-type notes.

effects.original_title: Distinction bias: Misprediction and mischoice due to joint evaluation
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.outcome: Predicted/experienced happiness (1-9) for quantitatively different tasks (25 vs 10 negative words; 10 vs 25 positive words)
effects.contrast: JE predicted-experience vs SE real-experience (and vs SE predicted-experience), differences between 25 vs 10 negative and 10 vs 25 positive word tasks
effects.timepoint: not applicable: single rating after task or prediction
effects.description: Original Study 2: people in joint evaluation overpredict the happiness difference between quantitatively different tasks (reading 25 vs 10 negative words, 10 vs 25 positive words) relative to people actually experiencing (or predicting) a single task in separate evaluation.
effects.citation_sentence: In the present paper, we report replications and extensions of Studies 1 and 2 from Hsee and Zhang (2004).
effects.evidence: Abstract: "Study 2 failed to find support for the original findings: People in JE did not consistently overpredict happiness for quantitatively different scenarios"; Study 2 Results: "The theoretical predictions were supported only in one out of four quantitative comparisons"; General Discussion: "In sum, we successfully replicated Study 1, from Hsee and Zhang (2004), but not Study 2."
effects.notes: Mixed pattern: JE overprediction vs SE real-experience arguably present for negative words (JE d = 0.45 sig, SE real ns), though the authors note the CIs overlap; absent for positive words (JE d = 0.02 ns) and absent vs SE predicted-experience for both. The authors' own summary for this hypothesis is 'failed to find support' / 'did not replicate', so failure; a second coder could choose inconclusive given 1 of 4 comparisons supported and the section's phrase 'results of Study 2 ... are inconclusive and, in general, do not replicate'. Study 2 also changed the procedure (read and copy-paste words online) in addition to MTurk population -> close extension.

effects.original_title: Distinction bias: Misprediction and mischoice due to joint evaluation
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.outcome: Predicted/experienced happiness (1-9) for qualitatively different tasks (10 negative vs 10 positive words)
effects.contrast: JE predicted-experience vs SE real-experience and vs SE predicted-experience, difference between 10 negative and 10 positive word tasks
effects.timepoint: not applicable: single rating after task or prediction
effects.description: Original Study 2: people in joint evaluation do not overpredict the happiness difference between qualitatively different tasks (10 negative vs 10 positive words), because people in separate evaluation (experiencing or predicting) also report significantly more happiness after positive words.
effects.citation_sentence: In the present paper, we report replications and extensions of Studies 1 and 2 from Hsee and Zhang (2004).
effects.evidence: Study 2 Results: "Thus, people in JE predictedexperience overpredicted the difference in happiness for the qualitatively different scenarios when compared to people in the SE real-experience, which is inconsistent with the theory of distinction bias ... but they did not overpredict the difference when compared to people in SE predicted-experience, which is consistent with the theory"; "...and in one of two qualitative comparisons (no overprediction ... in comparison to SE predicted-experience)".
effects.notes: Split result across the two SE comparison groups: consistent with original vs SE predicted-experience (both JE and SE-pred significant, CIs overlap), inconsistent vs SE real-experience (SE real d = 0.02 ns; JE overpredicted). Original described the focal comparison as JE predicted vs SE real-experience, which failed here, and the General Discussion lists this among three ways Study 2 'failed to support the distinction bias hypotheses' -> failure is a plausible alternative; coded inconclusive per the 1-of-2 split and the failure/inconclusive tiebreaker.
